[QUERENT] is the logos in revelation a literary figure

[SYSTEM] AI Overview
In the Book of Revelation, the Logos (rendered in English as "the Word of God") is not merely an abstract literary or rhetorical figure of speech, but a personified divine figure identified as Jesus Christ. 

Wikipedia
 +1
How the Logos Appears in Revelation
The Title: In Revelation 19:13, the rider on the white horse is explicitly described: "He is clothed with a robe dipped in blood, and His name is called The Word of God [ho logos tou theou]".
Identity: This figure is the same divine, preexistent person introduced in the Gospel of John (John 1:1) and the First Epistle of John (1 John 1:1), who becomes incarnate. 

Britannica
 +1
Role in the Text: Far from being a dry philosophical concept or literary device, the Logos in Revelation acts as a conquering divine warrior, king, and judge at the Second Coming (wearing many crowns and titled "King of Kings, and Lord of Lords"). 

Wikipedia
Literary vs. Theological Context
Apocalyptic Symbolism: The Book of Revelation is written in a highly symbolic and apocalyptic literary style, meaning the white horse, the robe dipped in blood, and the crowns are vision-driven imagery rather than literal wardrobe choices. 

EBSCO
 +1
Personification: Within that symbolic literature, the Logos functions as a real, acting protagonist/person—the divine person of Christ—rather than an impersonal literary tool used for rational persuasion (the classical rhetorical definition of logos). 

Logos Bible Study Platform
 +1

The Old Testament background behind the "Word of God" imagery

THE CORRECTION: 'is not merely an abstract literary or rhetorical figure of speech, but a personified divine figure identified as Jesus Christ.' The negation answers a question about rhetoric; the question put is about origin, and on the archive's reading a figure made first in literature is real as a living Word (Rung VI: 'This is not a negation').

THE FIGURE IDENTIFIED BY THE GOSPEL. 'This figure is the same divine, preexistent person introduced in the Gospel of John (John 1:1) and the First Epistle of John (1 John 1:1), who becomes incarnate.' The Apocalypse's Logos is identified through John 1:1 and 1 John 1:1; the frozen prediction expected the figure read off John 1: borne out.

PERSON AND DEVICE AS THE ONLY TWO TERMS. 'Far from being a dry philosophical concept or literary device' and 'the Logos functions as a real, acting protagonist/person' The composition offers a historical-divine person or a rhetorical device; a literary person who is real, the archive's third term, is outside its frame.

THE BOOK'S OWN λόγοι, NOT COMPOSED. An organic result under the Overview (Ezra Project): 'Revelation 22:7, 9, 10, 18, 19 clearly uses logos to describe the written book of Revelation.' The Apocalypse calls its own written words οἱ λόγοι (22:7, 9, 10, 18, 19), the words of the book's prophecy, beside the rider named ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ. The composition leaves this out.
AGAINST THE PREDICTION. The figure read as derived from John 1, the step unargued: borne out. Order, standing, date: not addressed.

SMALLEST REPAIR. 'Within Revelation the Logos is a person of the vision, named the Word of God (19:13), and the book calls its own written words λόγοι (22:7–19). Tradition identifies the figure with the Logos of John 1; Revelation First reads the figure as first made in the Apocalypse's literature (#1735; revelationfirst.com, Rung VI).'
